Sample.evidence_source: This study is based on in-depth interviews with fifty-two men who had attempted suicide.

Population.evidence_source: This study is based on in-depth interviews with fifty-two men who had attempted suicide.

Area.evidence_source: The focus in this paper is on non-disclosure ofdistress. Although some of the suicidal actions appeared to be relatively impulsive, the majority ofthe men had been considering suicide for some time. Reasons given for the action included generalised unhappiness about their lives, a feeling ofbeing trapped in a situation, relationship break-up, psychiatric illness and anger. Non-disclosure, the failure to divulge distress to others, emerged as a key issue in examining pathways to suicidal action for the men. Over two-thirds said they would never disclose emotional matters to anyone and none had spoken of the distress which led to the suicidal action. The reason for this was that they primarily viewed the disclosure of difficulties as un-masculine and as implying weakness. Furthermore, any show of weakness was associated with feminine or homosexual type behaviour. Constant performative work, including hyper-performances, was required to project this image of strength and to conceal growing levels of distress. As the men's fears and anxieties increased the opportunity for disclosure receded as the gap increased between the projected and the actual, vulnerable, self. Male friends were regarded as unreceptive to emotional communication and likely to reject confessional discourse. Communicating any psychological difficulties was regarded as taboo amongst men. An underlying fear around this type of communication with other men was that it might be perceived as homosexual discourse. The overall picture was of a rigidly defined performance of emotional inexpressiveness and a series of barriers preventing disclosure and inhibiting others from identifying problems. they felt constrained by hegemonic masculine expectations and their surrounding environment did not facilitate disclosure either. social isolation added an additional defensive element to them. The reasons for non-disclosure relate primarily to expectations around male behaviour. boys learn that 'it is unmanly to admit pain and request help' (2002: 80) are exactly borne out in this study. The outcome is a highly rehearsed and rigid performance enacted in the face of extensive personal difficulties. avoiding confessional discourse, creating masks to disguise distress, and, not infrequently, attempting to blunt uncomfortable emotions with drink or drugs. One ofthe key obstacles in understanding men and the meaning oftheir lives is their inscrutability and their fears of emotional transparency.
